rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means they would not believe or accept Moses as truthful.
rows.anchor: لن نؤمن لك أي لن نصدقك يقال آمن به وآمن له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing first means visual perception, then by extension knowledge; the verb also has distinct sight, opinion, and dream usages.
rows.anchor: والرؤية الإدراك بالبصر ثم يستعمل بمعنى العلم يقال رأى ببصره رؤية ورأى من الرأي رأيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raʾy can mean fine appearance and bearing; Jarir’s verse supplies an Arabic usage witness for raʾy.
rows.anchor: والرأي حسن الشارة والهيئة قال جرير:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jahr denotes appearance and open disclosure; the author distinguishes it from direct perception by relating them to the perceived object and perceiver.
rows.anchor: والجهر والعلامة والمعاينة نظائر يقال جهر بكلامه وبقراءته جهرا إذا علن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing may occur in sleep or by the heart, but jahra makes the seeing literal eyesight rather than imagination.
rows.anchor: وقد تكون الرؤية في المنام والرؤية بالقلب فإذا قال جهرة لم يكن إلا رؤية العين على التحقيق دون التخييل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāʿiqa has three senses: fire from heaven, death, or punishment, illustrated respectively by other Qurʾanic passages.
rows.anchor: والصاعقة على ثلاثة أوجه أحدها:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥattā means until, governs a noun, and makes narā subjunctive through an implicit an; the phrase is construed in the genitive and as the object of believe.
rows.anchor: حتى بمعنى إلى وهي الجارة للاسم

words: لَن نُّؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّىٰ نَرَى ٱللَّهَ جَهْرَةًۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest interpretation is that they would not accept Moses’ claim to be a commissioned prophet until God appeared openly and confirmed it.
rows.anchor: في قولك أنك نبي مبعوث

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation has them rejecting Moses’ account of God’s attributes and what may or may not be ascribed to Him until they see God.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه إنا لا نصدقك فيما تخبر به من صفات الله تعالى وما يجوز عليه وما لا يجوز عليه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view says they demanded to see God before believing that the Torah on the tablets came from God.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه لما جاءهم بالألواح وفيها التوراة قالوا لن نؤمن بأن هذا من عند الله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take jahra as modifying their public, outspoken address to Moses, rather than their seeing; the author prefers the first interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم إن قوله جهرة صفة لخطابهم لموسى أنهم جهروا به وأعلنوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ṣāʿiqa means death, and they watched the signs leading to death.
rows.anchor: إلى أسباب الموت وقيل إلى النار

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says they were watching the fire.
rows.anchor: وقيل إلى النار وإنما قرع الله سبحانه اليهود بسؤال أسلافهم الرؤية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews are rebuked for repeating their forebears’ resistance to the prophet they had to follow, including demands for another god, worship of the calf, and a demand to see God.
rows.anchor: وإنما قرع الله سبحانه اليهود بسؤال أسلافهم الرؤية من حيث إنهم سلكوا طريقتهم في المخالفة

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم البلخي
rows.claim: Al-Balkhi argues the verse rejects both their defiance of Moses and their allowance of vision of God, and cites 4:153 as corroboration.
rows.anchor: واستدل أبو القاسم البلخي بهذه الآية على أن الرؤية لا تجوز على الله تعالى قال لأنها إنكار

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم البلخي
rows.claim: He connects this demand with 4:153, where they asked Moses to show them God openly, as evidence that both parts of the demand are rejected.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد ذلك قوله تعالى فقد سألوا موسى أكبر من ذلك فقالوا أرنا الله جهرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Moses’ request to see God was made on behalf of his people; the Torah’s adherents agree he asked for vision only once, on their behalf.
rows.anchor: لأنه لا خلاف بين أهل التوراة أن موسى ع يسأل الرؤية إلا دفعة واحدة وهي التي سألها لقومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lightness is the opposite of heaviness; easing, lightening, and making something less severe are equivalent senses.
rows.anchor: اللغة: الخفة نقيض الثقل والتخفيف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One account explains heaviness and lightness through the decrease or increase of bodies.
rows.anchor: واختلف في الخفة والثقل فقيل إنه يرجع إلى تناقص الجواهر وتزايدها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account calls downward-directed dependence heaviness and upward-directed dependence lightness.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن الاعتماد اللازم سفلا يسمى ثقلا والاعتماد اللازم المختص بجهة العلو يسمى خفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These are the people just described as believing in part of the Book and disbelieving in part.
rows.anchor: أشار إلى الذين أخبر عنهم بأنهم يؤمنون ببعض الكتاب ويكفرون ببعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They traded away the bliss of the Hereafter prepared for believers in exchange for worldly leadership and its lowly benefits.
rows.anchor: جعل سبحانه تركهم حظوظهم من نعيم الآخرة بكفرهم بالله ثمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They have no share in the Hereafter’s bliss, and their punishment will neither be reduced nor made less severe.
rows.anchor: أي لا ينقص من عذابهم ولا يهون عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one will help them in the Hereafter by warding off God’s punishment.
rows.anchor: أي لا ينصرهم أحد في الآخرة فيدفع عنهم بنصرته

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads nunsikh with a damma on nūn and kasra on sīn; the other readers open both vowels.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر ما ننسخ بضم النون وكسر السين والباقون بفتحها

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read nansaʾhā with both vowels open and a hamza; the rest read nunshihā with a damma, kasra, and no hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ننساها بفتح النون والسين وإثبات الهمزة والباقون بضم النون وكسر السين بلا همز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best explanation of Ibn ʿĀmir’s form is that nasakha and ansakha are two synonymous dialect forms; the ordinary open-vowel reading is clearer.
rows.anchor: لغتين متفقتين في المعنى وإن اختلفتا في اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, naskh means removing something and putting another thing in its place, as the sun removes and replaces the shade.
rows.anchor: النسخ في اللغة إبطال شيء وإقامة آخر مقامه يقال نسخت الشمس الظل أي أذهبته وحلت محله

rows.speaker: ابن دريد
rows.claim: Ibn Durayd generalizes the root: anything that replaces another thing has superseded it.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن دريد كل شيء خلف شيئا فقد انتسخه وانتسخ الشيب الشباب

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Alī ibn ʿĪsā defines abrogation as lifting an obligation and replacing it, but the author rejects this as too broad, giving inability to pray standing and a ruling against reason as counterexamples.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بصحيح لأنه ينتقض بمن يلزمه الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrogation is a later legal proof that a ruling established by an earlier text will not apply in the future, though absent the later proof the earlier text would still govern.
rows.anchor: وأولى ما يجد به النسخ أن يقال هو كل دليل شرعي دل على أن مثل الحكم الثابت بالنص الأول غير ثابت في المستقبل

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: The first kind of Qurʾanic abrogation lifts both a verse’s ruling and its recitation; Abū Bakr is reported to have cited a formerly recited warning about disowning fathers.
rows.anchor: أن يرفع حكم الآية وتلاوتها كما روي عن أبي بكر أنه قال كنا نقرأ لا ترغبوا عن آبائكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second form of Qurʾanic abrogation leaves a verse written in the muṣḥaf while removing its legal force; 60:11 is the example.
rows.anchor: هذه ثابتة اللفظ في الخط مرتفعة الحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third form removes the wording while retaining the ruling, as with the stoning verse; the author notes many reports of recitations once present in the Qurʾan being lifted.
rows.anchor: ومنها ما يرتفع اللفظ ويثبت الحكم كآية الرجم فقد قيل كانت منزلة فرفع لفظها

rows.speaker: أبو موسى
rows.claim: Abū Mūsā reports a recitation that a person with two valleys of wealth would seek a third, that only dust fills his stomach, and that God accepts the repentance of the repentant; it was later lifted.
rows.anchor: ما روي عن أبي موسى أنهم كانوا يقرأون لو أن لابن آدم واديين من مال

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that a recitation honoring the seventy Anṣār killed at Biʾr Maʿūna was later lifted.
rows.anchor: وعن أنس أن السبعين من الأنصار الذين قتلوا ببئر معونة قرأنا فيهم كتابا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda interprets nansaʾhā as letting the verse proceed without abrogating it; Ṭarafa’s line uses the root for driving something along.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة معنى ننسأها أي نمضيها فلا ننسخها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root n-s-ʾ means delay: camels can be kept from the watering place or their watering interval extended; it also describes fattening livestock and urging a mount onward.
rows.anchor: نسأت الإبل في ظمئها أنسأها نسأ إذا زدتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā is a conditional noun standing in place of an, accusative as the object of nansakh but fronted because it represents a sentence-initial conditional particle; the verbs are jussive.
rows.anchor: ما اسم ناب مناب أن وهو في موضع نصب بننسخ وإنما لزمه التقديم وإن كان مفعولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in min āya is either partitive or redundant.
rows.anchor: ومن في قوله من آية للتبعيض وقيل هي مزيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alam is formally interrogative but functions as confirmation, and taʿlam remains jussive under lam because the interrogative does not change the governing particle’s effect.
rows.anchor: ولفظ ألم ها هنا لفظ الاستفهام ومعناه التقرير وتعلم مجزوم بلم

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: One coherence reading sees the verse assuring believers that God will still send them good despite disbelievers’ wish that no good be revealed to them.
rows.anchor: دل بهذه الآية على أنه سبحانه لا يخليهم من إنزال خير إليهم

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim reads the verse as a reply to Jews who criticized Muhammad for abrogating previous religious laws.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه سبحانه لما عاب اليهود بأشياء ورد عليهم ما راموا به الطعن في أمر نبينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse may mean whatever verse or ruling God removes, or whatever verse He replaces, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: قد ذكرنا حقيقة النسخ عند المحققين وقيل معناه ما نرفع من آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading nunsihā has two possible senses: forgetting, the opposite of remembering, or leaving and abandoning.
rows.anchor: فالوجه الأول في الآية مروي عن قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forgetfulness sense is illustrated by the command to remember God if one forgets, while abandonment is illustrated by God abandoning those who abandon Him.
rows.anchor: أي تركوا طاعة الله فترك رحمتهم أو ترك تخليصهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda applies forgetfulness to the community: they may be told to leave off reciting a verse until they forget it; Abū Jaʿfar says this should not apply to the Prophet lest it repel people.
rows.anchor: الوجه الأول في الآية مروي عن قتادة وهو أن يكون محمولا على النسيان

rows.speaker: جماعة من المحققين
rows.claim: Other scholars allow God to make even the Prophet forget a verse when public interest requires it, including by miraculously causing a large group to forget together.
rows.anchor: وقد جوز جماعة من المحققين ذلك على النبي

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the Prophet was taught the Qurʾan and then forgot it, citing God’s promise to make him recite without forgetting except what God wills.
rows.anchor: ذهب الحسن فقال: إن نبيكم أقرىء القرآن

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj rejects interpreting the word as forgetting because 17:73 and 17:86 say God would not will to remove what He revealed to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وأنكر الزجاج هذا القول فقال

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī answers that the cited verses concern reports and histories that cannot be abrogated, whereas the Prophet could forget commands whose ruling depends on changing circumstances.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي الفارسي هذا الذي احتج به على من ذهب إلى أن ننسها من النسيان لا يدل على فساد ما ذهبوا إليه

rows.speaker: سعد بن أبي وقاص وسالم مولى أبي حذيفة وسعد بن مالك
rows.claim: Variants from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Sālim, and Saʿd ibn Mālik read the form as making someone forget; their wording supports the forgetfulness interpretation.
rows.anchor: قراءة سعد بن أبي وقاص وقراءة من قرأ أو ننسكها وهو المروي عن سالم مولى أبي حذيفة

rows.speaker: الضحاك وابن مسعود والأعمش ومجاهد عن أبي
rows.claim: Readings attributed to al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Masʿūd, al-Aʿmash, and Ubayy render the omitted object as the Prophet or someone being made to forget the verse.
rows.anchor: ما روي عن الضحاك أنه قرأ ننسها ويؤكد ذلك أيضا ما روي من قراءة ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the reading nunsihā the intended object is omitted; the explicit object in nunsikhā makes the meaning of causing someone to forget clear.
rows.anchor: فالمفعول المراد المحذوف في قراءة من قرأ أو ننسها مظهر في قراءة من قرأ ننسكها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda also says verses used to be abrogated by other verses and that God caused His Prophet to forget some of them.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة أنه قال كانت الآية تنسخ بالآية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās takes nunsihā to mean abandonment: God commands people to leave off acting on the verse.
rows.anchor: والوجه الثاني وهو أن المراد بالنسيان الترك في الآية مروي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the sense ‘abandon’ is expressed with nasītu, not ansaytu; the verse means God commands people to leave the verse.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج إنما يقال في هذا نسيت إذا تركت ولا يقال فيه أنسيت تركت

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says interpreting ansaytu as ‘left’ is not wrong, since a person commanded to leave something has in effect left it.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي من فسر أنسيت بتركت لا يكون مخطئا لأنك إذا أنسيت فقد نسيت

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Alī ibn ʿĪsā explains that commentators describe the resulting meaning: one commanded to leave the verse has left it.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا قال علي بن عيسى إنما فسره المفسرون على ما يؤول إليه المعنى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Leaving the verse means preserving it without abrogation, as Ibn ʿAbbās explains: leave it and do not replace it; God’s ‘leaving’ is an expansive expression for letting something be.
rows.anchor: وإنما معناه اقرارها فلا ترفع كما قال ابن عباس نتركها فلا نبدلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For readers who vocalize the word as nansaʾhā, with the sense of delay, the author lays out four interpretations.
rows.anchor: وأما من قرأ أو ننسأها على معنى التأخير فقيل فيه وجوه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view means delaying a verse’s revelation and sending a replacement that serves the same interest or is better for people.
rows.anchor: أن معناه أو نؤخرها فلا ننزلها وننزل بدلا منها مما يقوم مقامها في المصلحة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view delays the verse to a later time and supplies an equivalent replacement at the earlier time; the author considers this the strongest account.
rows.anchor: أن معناه نؤخرها إلى وقت ثان ونأتي بدلا منها في الوقت المتقدم بما يقوم مقامها

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A third view treats delay as a verse’s recitation being lifted after revelation and practice; Ubayy reports that al-Aḥzāb once had more than seventy verses and exceeded al-Baqara in length.
rows.anchor: أن أبيا قال له:

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid’s fourth view leaves the written wording and recitation in place while abrogating the ruling.
rows.anchor: وهو ما حكي عن مجاهد يثبت خطها ويبدل حكمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author favors the second view; the first has little purpose if people never knew or heard the delayed verse, while the last two simply amount to abrogation.
rows.anchor: والوجهان الأولان عليهما الاعتماد لأن الوجهين الأخرين يرجع معناهما إلى معنى النسخ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One interpretation takes ‘better’ as easier for people, such as the eased fighting command, and ‘equal’ as equally easy, such as changing the prayer direction to the Kaaba; this is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: في السهولة كالعبادة بالتوجه إلى الكعبة بعد أن كان إلى بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says a replacement is better or equal in the later period because it better serves the public interest of that time.
rows.anchor: نأت بخير منها في الوقت الثاني أي هي لكم في الوقت الثاني خير لكم من الأولى في الوقت الأول

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take the address as directed to the Prophet; others take it to all morally responsible people, meaning any listener or person.
rows.anchor: قيل هو خطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وقيل هو خطاب لجميع المكلفين والمراد ألم تعلم أيها السامع

words: أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ قَدِيرٌ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one reading, God can produce verses and sūras like the Qurʾan to replace an abrogated command with something equally beneficial.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى قادر على آيات وسور مثل القرآن ينسخ بها ما أمر فيقوم في النفع مقام المنسوخ

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: If addressed to Muhammad, the question means God can help him and defeat his enemies; another view makes it general to everything.
rows.anchor: وعلى القول الأول معناه ألم تعلم يا محمد أنه سبحانه قادر على نصرك والانتصار لك من أعدائك

rows.speaker: من زعم أنه لا يجوز نسخ القرآن بالسنة المعلومة
rows.claim: Those denying abrogation of Qurʾan by definitive Sunna argue that the verse attributes the replacement to God, while Sunna is not literally attributed to Him, and that the verse concerns God’s unique power over the miraculous Qurʾan.
rows.anchor: واستدل من زعم أنه لا يجوز نسخ القرآن بالسنة المعلومة بهذه الآية قال أضاف الإتيان بخير منها إلى نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author holds that definitive Sunna may abrogate Qurʾan: it comes by God’s revelation and command, and ‘better’ means more beneficial for faith and reward, whether delivered by Qurʾan or Sunna.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن القرآن يجوز أن ينسخ بالسنة المقطوع عليها ومعنى خير منها أي أصلح لنا منها في ديننا

words: أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ قَدِيرٌ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shows the Qurʾan is created and distinct from God: an eternal thing cannot be abrogated, and anything under God’s power is an originated act.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه الآية دلالة على أن القرآن محدث وأنه غير الله تعالى لأن القديم لا يصح نسخه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAzīz can mean unconquerable, or capable of anything He wills with nothing able to prevent Him; the root also conveys victory, hardness, rarity, and honor through association.
rows.anchor: الذي لا يغالب وقيل هو القادر الذي لا يمتنع عليه شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥakīm means the one who directs and makes creation well, an attribute of action; it can also mean all-knowing, an attribute of essence.
rows.anchor: والحكيم معناه المدبر الذي يحكم الصنع ويحسن التدبير فعلى هذا يكون من صفات الفعل وبكون بمعنى العليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibʿath is a verbal clause coordinated with tab; fīhim attaches to ibʿath or to an omitted ‘messenger being among them’ and then functions circumstantially.
rows.anchor: ابعث جملة فعلية معطوفة على تب فيهم تتعلق بابعث ويجوز أن تتعلق بمحذوف تقديره رسولا كائنا فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yatlū is accusative as an adjective of rasūlan, while ʿalayhim attaches to yatlū.
rows.anchor: ويتلو منصوب الموضع بكونه صفة قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fīhim refers to the Muslim community among Abraham’s descendants, especially his Meccan descendants; the messenger is Muhammad, the only one sent from them.
rows.anchor: الضمير في قولهم فيهم يرجع إلى الأمة المسلمة التي سأل الله إبراهيم أن يجعلهم من ذريته

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وجماعة من العلماء
rows.claim: Ḥasan, Qatāda, and other scholars identify the requested messenger as Muhammad, who said he was Abraham’s prayer and Jesus’ good tidings, referring to Jesus’ prediction of a messenger named Aḥmad.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الحسن وقتادة وجماعة من العلماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reciting God’s signs means reading the revelations He sends down to the messenger.
rows.anchor: أي يقرأ عليهم آياتك التي توحي بها إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book is the Qurʾan; teaching it is not redundant with recitation, since recitation shows its miraculous proof of prophethood while teaching explains monotheism, its evidence, and the law.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يعد من التكرار لأنه خص الأول بالتلاوة ليعلموا بذلك أنه معجز دال على صدقه ونبوته

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets wisdom here as the Sunna.
rows.anchor: قيل هي ها هنا السنة عن قتادة

rows.speaker: مالك بن أنس
rows.claim: Mālik ibn Anas explains wisdom as knowledge of religion and understanding its interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل المعرفة بالدين والفقه في التأويل عن مالك بن أنس

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes wisdom as knowledge of rulings that can be learned only from the messengers.
rows.anchor: وقيل العلم بالأحكام التي لا يدرك علمها إلا من قبل الرسل عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One grammatical reading makes wisdom an adjective of the Book, so it is characterized as Book, wisdom, and signs.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنه صفة للكتاب كأنه وصفه بأنه كتاب وأنه حكمة وأنه آيات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view calls wisdom a light God places in the heart, enabling understanding as eyesight enables seeing.
rows.anchor: وقيل الحكمة شيء يجعله الله في القلب ينوره الله به كما ينور البصر

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil interprets wisdom as Qurʾanic admonitions and knowledge of its lawful and prohibited matters.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي مواعظ القرآن وحرامه وحلاله عن مقاتل وكل حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the messenger makes people obedient and sincere; zakāʾ means obedience and sincerity toward God.
rows.anchor: والزكاء هو الطاعة والإخلاص لله سبحانه عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says purification means cleansing people of idolatry.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه يطهرهم من الشرك ويخلصهم منه عن ابن جريج

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī interprets purification as calling people to faith and righteous acts through which they become pure.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه يستدعيهم إلى فعل ما يزكون به من الإيمان والصلاح عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm says purification means the messenger will testify on Judgment Day that they were pure, when every soul is judged by what it earned.
rows.anchor: وقيل يشهد لهم بأنهم أزكياء يوم القيامة إذا شهد على كل نفس بما كسبت عن الأصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names mean complete power and majesty, and mastery over the wonders of creation; they suit the prayer because God can answer and knows hidden thoughts and what benefits people.
rows.anchor: أي القوي في كمال قدرتك المنيع في جلال عظمتك المحكم لبدائع صنعتك وإنما ذكر هاتين الصفتين لاتصالهما بالدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer asks for all conditions of prophethood: recitation entails conveying revelation, teaching entails explaining it, and wisdom entails the Sunna.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه الآية دلالة على أن إبراهيم وإسماعيل ع دعوا لنبينا محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم بجميع شرائط النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer also seeks divine grace for the community, enabling them to hold to scripture and law and become pure; because Ishmael made the prayer, the promised prophet is his descendant, Muhammad, the only prophet from Ishmael’s line.
rows.anchor: فصاروا أزكياء وهذا لأن الدعاء صدر من إسماعيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿrūf is just conduct that cannot rightly be condemned and contains no unfairness or injustice.
rows.anchor: المعروف هو العدل الذي لا يجوز أن ينكر ولا حيف فيه ولا جور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥuḍūr means that something is present in a way that can be perceived.
rows.anchor: والحضور وجود الشيء بحيث يمكن أن يدرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaqq can mean an act that cannot be denied, or anything known to be sound as a statement, act, or belief; it is the verbal noun of ḥaqqa.
rows.anchor: والحق هو الفعل الذي لا يجوز إنكاره وقيل هو ما علم صحته سواء كان قولا أو فعلا أو اعتقادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kutiba ʿalaykum means ‘and it was prescribed’; the conjunction is omitted because the prior account is complete and this account connects through its subject matter.
rows.anchor: قوله كتب عليكم المعنى وكتب عليكم إلا أن الكلام إذا طال استغنى عن العطف بالواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-waṣiyya is nominative either as the passive subject of kutiba or as a subject whose predicate is li-l-wālidayn; in the latter parse the statement is quoted as what was prescribed.
rows.anchor: والوصية ارتفعت لأحد وجهين إما بأنه اسم ما لم يسم فاعله وهو كتب وإما بأنه مبتدأ وقوله للوالدين خبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The time phrase may attach to kutiba, placing the duty at the onset of illness, or follow al-Zajjāj’s parse: make a will while healthy for implementation when death comes.
rows.anchor: وأما العامل في إذا ففيه وجهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaqqan can be an emphatic verbal noun, a circumstantial adjective meaning ‘rightful’, or a verbal noun from kataba meaning ‘a written obligation’.
rows.anchor: وحقا نصب على المصدر وتقديره أحق ذلك حقا وقد استعمل على وجه الصفة بمعنى ذي الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse establishes the law of bequests; ‘when death comes’ means its causes, such as illness or old age, not the moment when death is directly witnessed and the dying person is too occupied to dictate a will.
rows.anchor: أي أسباب الموت من مرض ونحوه من الهرم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes the bequest obligatory while a person is healthy, with instructions for what should happen when death arrives.
rows.anchor: وقيل فرض عليكم الوصية في حال الصحة أن تقولوا إذا حضرنا الموت فافعلوا كذا

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī says the bequest is due for any amount of property, little or much.
rows.anchor: فقال الزهري في القليل والكثير مما يقع عليه اسم المال

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī sets the relevant property threshold at one thousand to five hundred dirhams.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم النخعي من ألف درهم إلى خمسمائة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās sets the threshold at eight hundred dirhams.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس إلى ثمانمائة درهم

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī visited a sick client with six or seven hundred dirhams, advised him not to make a will because he did not have much wealth, and the author says this is the adopted position among his school.
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي ع أنه دخل على مولى له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fair dealing may refer to a proportionate bequest, since a wealthy person’s bequest of one dirham is not fair, or to choosing recipients justly; both readings apply.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يرجع ذلك إلى قدر ما يوصي لأن من يملك المال الكثير إذا أوصى بدرهم فلم يوص بالمعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fair distribution also requires not preferring the rich over the poor or a more distant relative over a closer one.
rows.anchor: أن يوصي للغني ويترك الفقير ويوصي للقريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘a duty upon the God-fearing’ emphasizes that the bequest is obligatory for those who choose piety.
rows.anchor: أي حقا واجبا على من آثر التقوى وهذا تأكيد في الوجوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Three positions are reported: the verse is abrogated, it is abrogated only for heirs but remains for non-heirs, or it is not abrogated; the author endorses the last view.
rows.anchor: واختلف في هذه الآية فقيل إنها منسوخة وقيل إنها منسوخة في المواريث ثابتة في غير الوارث وقيل إنها غير منسوخة أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers that the verse remains in force: inheritance and bequest rulings do not conflict, and abrogation requires that the two rulings cannot both be followed.
rows.anchor: وهو الصحيح عند المحققين من أصحابنا لأن من قال إنها منسوخة بآية المواريث فقوله باطل بأن النسخ بين الخبرين إنما يكون إذا تنافى العمل بموجبهما
